thread.title: The 1 Essential Item Your Retirement Portfolio Is Probably Missing: Asset Allocation Daily

author: SA For FAs
title: The 1 Essential Item Your Retirement Portfolio Is Probably Missing: Asset Allocation Daily
text:
Short-Term Bonds “The ETF ( IEI ) has an effective duration of 4.4 and offers a yield of 2.83%, just below the cycle high of roughly 3% but if short-term rates have topped out, the chance to capture nearly a 3% yield with limited downside and large potential capital appreciation will not last long. Investors often underestimate the capital appreciation that can come with Treasury bonds in addition to the yield. If timed properly, and the cycle high for rates has been made, even short-term bonds such as 5-year Treasuries can offer over 20% gains.” ( Eric Basmajian )
Value In S&P 500’s Biggest Laggards? “The laggards were led by Pacific Gas & Electric ( PCG ), which saw roughly half its value erased as the company is investigated for its role in the devastating and tragic Camp Fire. General Electric ( GE ) continued one if the worst years in its long and storied history, finishing as the third worst performer on the month. Apple ( AAPL ), was the 10th worst performer on the month, weighing on the broad market gauge and helping the equal-weighted index ( RSP ) to outperform the capitalization weighted index on the month.” ( Ploutos )
U.S.-China Soybeans “The White House statement does say that China agreed to buy a "substantial" amount of US agricultural products from US farmers immediately. However there was no mention of what "substantial" means, whilst the Chinese statement does not specify what specific goods they agreed to purchase, and under what timeframe.” ( ING Economic and Financial Analysis )
How To Think About Annuities “Think about the following ‘allocation’ question: should you include phosphorus or zinc supplements in your ‘portfolio’ of daily pills? Well, if your regular diet consists of plenty of peas (phosphorus) and shellfish (zinc), then you are probably consuming more than the recommended milligrams per day. There’s no need for more. But if you don’t (or can’t) enjoy those foods, or other dishes heavy in phosphorus and zinc, you should consider supplements. But remember, 700 milligrams of phosphorus per day is a good idea, 7,000 is unhealthy and 70,000 will incinerate your internal organs and kill you. My point? The role of annuities in the optimal retirement portfolio is similar to the role of these minerals and elements. A well-balanced daily diet includes a cocktail of copper, iron, phosphorus, and zinc. All diversified retirement portfolios should consist of some cash, stocks, bonds, real estate, health insurance, long-term care insurance, and some—but not too much—annuities. I like to think of it as a retirement cocktail.” (Moshe Milevsky, writing in the Journal of Financial Planning )
Thought For The Day If your specific financial challenge is how to obtain a retirement income that you cannot outlive, then ownership of the right kind of annuity might be an important part of the solution. So says York University finance professor Moshe Milevsky in a lengthy journal article (linked above) that’s worth every minute of the time of anyone grappling with how to fund his or her retirement. The article demythologizes a financial product that is too often credited with little more than half its true number of letters, which is to say it is seen as being a dirty word – something that people should “hate.” Milevsky points out that hating annuities makes as much sense as hating a “fund” – a category that includes hedge funds, mutual funds, index funds, private equity funds, exchange-traded funds and more, some of which may be quite lovable.
Milevsky doesn’t come at this issue as an industry shill (he discloses, at the top rather than bottom of his article, that he serves on the board of Cannex Financial, though he is primarily an academic), but as a finance scholar, and he humorously recounts his first roadshow showing off his early research aimed at minimizing the problem of portfolio ruin, mainly by increasing retirees’ exposure to stocks. His fancy equations didn’t add up for an audience of financial services professionals, who thought that an annuity might neatly solve the problem.
Annuities were not then, nor now, an important part of the biz school curriculum, so he didn’t quite know how to process the feedback. What changed his thinking on this topic (and the thinking of many other top finance scholars) was a seminal paper written by Menahem Yaari in 1965, when the Israeli economist was teaching at Stanford and Yale. Yaari demonstrated that no investment could outperform an annuity if the problem in need of a solution was smoothing out lifetime income.
I’ll get to why this is shortly, but not before noting my favorite part of Milevsky’s article (which is a tough call, because the article is laden with insight and so nicely written): Many of those who have some familiarity with annuities as academics or financial professionals have heard of Yaari, but may not know – I did not – that his famous contribution to the field consists of just one 13-page article written over half a century ago. He went on to many other important areas of research, such as in decision theory, but his oft-cited annuity work was just that single item. Of this curiosity, Milevsky writes the following two sentences:
Some might call it a one-hit wonder, but what a song! My understanding is that he claimed, when asked, that he didn’t think he had much to add to that classic 1965 paper.”
The first sentence is cute, but the second – that Yaari felt he didn’t have much to add – is highly significant. That is because the simplest truths need little elaboration. We would all be better off if writers (yours truly included) restricted themselves to what is truly important. I first heard this point made by Milevsky himself the last time I had the pleasure of meeting with him in person. He is one of the rare academics whose work is consistently interesting, and Yaari, evidently, personifies academic humility.
So why then is the utility of an annuity product so obvious as to need little elaboration. It is because the provider must keep on sending you the same annuity payment as long as you live, be that to age 70, 80, 90, 100 or beyond. As Milevsky puts it:
I like to explain it as having a mortgage on your house that never matures. As long as you are still alive, you have to make mortgage payments to the bank. No matter how much you have already paid, it’s never over. This sounds horribly usurious and unappealing, but reverse the image and you will understand how the basic (academic) annuity works. The insurance company has to make payments to you forever; it never ends as long as you are alive. That’s something I can live with.”
Milevsky makes it clear that such a product is not relevant to Warren Buffett, Ken Fisher, Steve Forbes or other billionaires. But for the majority of people whose resources are not large enough to remove the doubt about whether they will last a lifetime, annuities make a lot of sense. Once you appreciate that unique advantage, then the matter of equipping your portfolio with longevity protection comes down to finding the right product and suitable service. Much of the “hatred” for annuities stems from high commissions, surrender changes and other opaque product features that have nothing to do with what Yaari, Milevsky and other financial economists admire and recommend. For insight into some of those details, read his thoroughly enjoyable article. If you do, you’ll find that lovable annuities exist and may be the one thing your retirement portfolio was missing.
